scribe_response.text: Can you tell me about the home you grew up in? I grew up in Iloilo, in a little wooden house beside the river. My father built it himself with timber left over from, from the boats he repaired. It stood on tall posts, because every rainy um season the river crept under the floor. When I was small, I thought the water was a friendly um neighbor visiting us. We had two rooms, a kitchen at the back, and a bamboo porch. All six children slept in one room, lined up on mats like sardines. My mother hung a mosquito net over us, and it smelled of smoke and soap. In the morning the sun, the sun um came through the gaps and drew stripes on the floor. I used to count those stripes before anyone else woke up. The kitchen was my mother's kingdom, with a clay stove and a blackened pot. She woke before dawn to cook rice and prepare the cakes she sold at market. The smell of coconut milk and sticky rice pulled us all out of bed. My father kept his tools under the house, wrapped in old flour uh sacks. There were chisels, planes, and a heavy mallet that I was never allowed to touch. What happened next? Sometimes I sat on a bucket and watched him shape a plank into a boat. He whistled while he worked, always the same slow tune about a fisherman and the moon. Our mango tree stood in front, and my brother Nestor climbed it like a monkey. In April the fruit turned golden, and the whole street argued over the first um ripe one. We also kept three chickens, one pig, and a rooster named General who hated me. Every morning he chased me to the well, and every morning I screamed. Four families shared the well, and all the uh gossip of the street was traded there. I carried water in a dented tin pail, and um my arms ached all the way home. When the typhoon season came, the sky turned the color of an old bruise. The wind rattled the tin roof so loudly that uh we could not hear each other. My um mother lit a candle before a picture of the Holy Child, and we prayed. My father tied the boats tight to the posts and checked the knots again and again. One night the river rose so high that it touched our first step. We climbed to the little attic and ate cold rice with dried fish by candlelight. Can you tell me more about that? I was frightened, was frightened, but my sister Luz told ghost stories until we laughed instead. In the morning the water, water went down and left brown mud on everything. We scrubbed the floor with coconut um husks, and it smelled of wet earth for a week. After supper the neighbors gathered on our uh porch to talk and share palm wine. We children chased fireflies along the riverbank with empty jam jars. My grandmother sat in her rocking chair, chewing betel nut and humming old songs. She had a face um like a um dried mango, but her eyes were bright and quick. She taught me to sew on a button, and that small skill carried me through life. The house had uh no electricity until I was nine, so we lived by oil lamps. When the first bulb glowed in our kitchen, my mother cried and my father laughed at her. I think of that house almost every day, even now in Abu Dhabi. Sometimes I close my eyes and hear the river slapping against the posts. I can smell the rice cakes and feel the warm bamboo under my bare feet. It was a poor house, but it was full um of music and noise and love.
